location: Karbala (the plain of al-Taff), on the western side of the Euphrates in Iraq, north-west of Kufa

date.note: 10 Muharram 61 AH, corresponding to 10 October 680 CE, the day of Ashura. Al-Tabari records this date on the authority of Abu Ma'shar, al-Waqidi (who called it the best-confirmed report), and Hisham ibn al-Kalbi; he also records a report from al-Waqidi, via Ibn Sa'd, placing the killing in Safar 61/November 680, and a variant on whether the day was a Saturday or a Friday. Al-Husayn's journey from Mecca toward Kufa and his arrival at Karbala on 2 Muharram 61/2 October 680 preceded the battle.

summary: At Karbala in Iraq, on 10 Muharram 61/10 October 680, al-Husayn ibn Ali, grandson of the Prophet Muhammad, and a small company of family members and supporters were killed by a much larger force sent by Ubayd Allah ibn Ziyad, governor of Kufa under the Umayyad caliph Yazid I, after al-Husayn had refused allegiance to Yazid. The event is central to Shi'i religious memory, commemorated annually on Ashura, and is also remembered, with different emphases, in Sunni tradition.
description: On the death of the caliph Mu'awiya in 60/680, his son Yazid sought the oath of allegiance from leading figures in the Hijaz, among them al-Husayn ibn Ali and Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, both of whom withheld it; al-Husayn withdrew to Mecca. According to the early reports preserved by al-Tabari, principally that of Abu Mikhnaf, the sequence of events was as follows. Receiving letters from Kufans inviting him to lead them, he sent his cousin Muslim ibn Aqil ahead to gauge support. Yazid appointed Ubayd Allah ibn Ziyad governor of Kufa; Ibn Ziyad suppressed the movement and had Muslim ibn Aqil executed. Al-Husayn set out from Mecca for Iraq with members of his household and a small following, was intercepted by Umayyad cavalry, and halted near Karbala, on the western side of the Euphrates, on 2 Muharram 61 (at a spot the report names al-'Aqr). A force commanded by Umar ibn Sa'd was sent against him, and negotiations over whether he would submit to Ibn Ziyad failed. The reports describe his camp as cut off from access to the river water in the days before the battle. On 10 Muharram 61/10 October 680 (the day of Ashura) the two sides fought; al-Husayn and most of the men with him were killed, and the women and children of his household, together with his son Ali ibn al-Husayn, were taken captive to Kufa and then to Yazid in Damascus, along with the heads of the dead. The principal account, transmitted by Abu Mikhnaf (d. 157/774) through Hisham ibn al-Kalbi and preserved by al-Tabari, puts al-Husayn's force on the morning of the battle at thirty-two horsemen and forty foot soldiers and reports seventy-two of his followers killed and eighty-eight killed on the side of Umar ibn Sa'd; another report in the same collection counts seventy heads brought to Ibn Ziyad by tribe. These figures are those of the early reports and vary among the sources; the size of the Umayyad force is also given differently. Modern scholars read the accounts as combining a historical core, which the Abu Mikhnaf material is generally held to preserve, with a growing hagiographical literature, some of it circulating under Abu Mikhnaf's name. In Shi'i tradition the killing of al-Husayn, regarded as the third imam in Twelver and Zaydi reckoning (the second in Nizari Isma'ili reckoning), became a central religious event. Twelver Shi'is understand his death as a voluntary sacrifice in the cause of truth and justice against tyranny, and devotional literature and theology attribute to it a redemptive significance, including the intercession of al-Husayn for those who mourn him. Its annual commemoration in the first ten days of Muharram, culminating on Ashura, includes public mourning assemblies, recitation of elegies and of the narrative of the martyrdom (maqtal), passion plays (ta'ziya), processions, and pilgrimage (ziyara) to his shrine at Karbala. Scholars such as Najam Haider and Heinz Halm also trace the role of the memory of Karbala in the formation of a distinct Shi'i communal identity, from the penitential Tawwabun movement of 65/684-85 onward. Sunni tradition also regards al-Husayn as a grandson of the Prophet and a Companion, and many Sunni authors lament his killing; Sunni Muslims have commonly marked Ashura primarily as a day of recommended fasting, which Sunni hadith (for example in Sahih al-Bukhari) associate with the Prophet's fasting on the day on which, by the report, God delivered the Israelites under Moses, and have generally not adopted the Shi'i ritual forms of mourning. Sunni scholars have differed in their assessment of Yazid's personal responsibility and standing. The event is thus a shared point of historical memory whose religious meaning Shi'i and Sunni communities articulate differently; this entry records each reading as that community's own.
editorial_notes: This entry is written under neutrality principles #1, #2, #4, and #7. The narrative core (Yazid's accession, the Kufan invitation, Muslim ibn Aqil, the interception, the battle on 10 Muharram 61, the captivity of the survivors and the transport of the heads) is explicitly framed as the account of the early reports preserved by al-Tabari, so that it is attributed rather than stated in editorial voice, and casualty figures are stated as the figures of those reports, with the variant count noted, rather than as established fact. Devotional vocabulary is kept out of editorial voice: the Shi'i understanding of al-Husayn's death as martyrdom (shahada) with redemptive and intercessory significance is stated as attributed belief, drawing on Ayoub's study of Twelver devotional literature, and the Sunni commemoration and assessment are stated as attributed practice and opinion. No judgment is made on the legitimacy of Yazid's caliphate or of al-Husayn's uprising. The remark on hagiographical elaboration and on a pseudonymous text attributed to Abu Mikhnaf follows the translator I. K. A. Howard's discussion of al-Tabari's sources, and is a statement about the textual tradition, not about any community's beliefs. The Sunni-memory paragraph is deliberately cautious and general, since Sunni positions on Yazid range widely; it is sourced to Afsaruddin and to Haider's comparative treatment. No compares_with link is given: a comparison of martyrdom memory across traditions was considered and set aside because no existing entry offered a sufficiently parallel question. Sources triangulate three lenses per principles #8 and #9: Western academic scholarship (Haider; Halm), the classical primary chronicle (al-Tabari, SUNY vol. 19, transmitting Abu Mikhnaf), and modern Muslim scholarship from Shi'i and Sunni vantages (Ayoub; Jafri; Afsaruddin). No encyclopedias are cited; the encyclopedia references inside the SUNY translator's footnotes are not relied on. Confidence: al-Tabari vol. 19 is rated high because the cited passages were read directly (Translator's Foreword pp. ix-xi; p. 82 and p. 91 on the date; p. 120 on al-Husayn's force; pp. 163-64 and 179 on the casualty and head counts); the other sources were verified to exist and treat the topic but were not read line by line, so they are rated medium. Dates are given in hijri and CE. Imam numbering is given per branch (al-Husayn third for Twelvers and Zaydis, second for Nizari Isma'ilis; Ja'far al-Sadiq sixth for Twelvers, fifth for Nizari Isma'ilis). The Shi'i primary voice is added through al-Shaykh al-Mufid's Kitab al-Irshad (medium, not read line by line), and the Sunni Ashura fast is sourced to Sahih al-Bukhari 2004, read directly in translation (high).

relations.note: The Umayyad accession that closed the First Fitna (656-661) and Mu'awiya's designation of his son Yazid as successor form the background to al-Husayn's refusal of allegiance in 60/680.

Al-Husayn was the son of Ali ibn Abi Talib and Fatima, the Prophet's daughter; Twelver and Zaydi Shi'is regard him as the third imam after Ali and his elder brother al-Hasan, while Nizari Isma'ilis count him as the second imam.

The killing of al-Husayn and its annual commemoration on Ashura are central to Shi'i religious memory and ritual, and scholarship traces the role of Karbala in the consolidation of Shi'i communal identity.
In Twelver Shi'ism al-Husayn is the third of the twelve imams; the Muharram mourning rites, the maqtal literature, and pilgrimage to his shrine at Karbala are major expressions of Twelver piety.
Shi'i tradition reads al-Husayn's stand as that of the rightful imam against an illegitimate ruler; the event is a reference point in the Shi'i doctrine of the imamate.

Sunni tradition honors al-Husayn as the Prophet's grandson and a Companion and many Sunni authors lament his killing, while commonly marking Ashura as a day of fasting rather than through the Shi'i mourning rites; Sunni scholars differ in their assessment of Yazid.
Ja'far al-Sadiq was a great-grandson of al-Husayn through al-Husayn's surviving son Ali ibn al-Husayn; he is revered as the sixth imam in Twelver reckoning and the fifth in Nizari Isma'ili reckoning.

Classical chronicle preserving the account of Abu Mikhnaf (via Hisham ibn al-Kalbi) and a report attributed to Muhammad al-Baqir; Translator's Foreword pp. ix-xi (the sources and hagiographical accretions), pp. 82 and 91 (date of 10 Muharram 61, and on p. 82 al-Waqidi's variant placing it in Safar 61), p. 120 (thirty-two horsemen and forty foot soldiers), pp. 163-64 (seventy-two of al-Husayn's followers and eighty-eight of Umar ibn Sa'd's killed; seventy-two heads), and p. 179 (seventy heads by tribe) were read directly. The primary-text lens.
